meta.title: Using Fire Extinguishers
meta.description: Covers fire classes, portable fire extinguisher types and labels, the P.A.S.S. technique, pre-use decision-making, inspection requirements, and when to evacuate instead of fight a fire.

fire-basics.title: How Fires Burn
fire-basics.content: Fires require three elements to burn: heat, fuel, and oxygen. Modern fire science also recognizes a continuing chemical chain reaction as a fourth element. Removing any one of these elements can extinguish a fire. Fires can grow rapidly, and what begins as a small controllable fire can spread and become life-threatening within seconds. Understanding how fires start and spread helps workers make faster and safer decisions during an emergency.

fire-classes.title: Fire Classes and Extinguishing Agents
fire-classes.content: Not all fires are the same. Using the wrong extinguisher can make a fire worse or place the employee in greater danger. Class A fires involve ordinary combustibles such as paper, cardboard, wood, cloth, and some plastics. Class B fires involve flammable liquids and gases. Class C fires involve energized electrical equipment. Class D fires involve combustible metals. Class K fires involve commercial cooking oils and fats. Each class requires a specific type of extinguishing agent.

extinguisher-types-labels.title: Types of Fire Extinguishers and Label Markings
extinguisher-types-labels.content: Common extinguisher types include water, dry chemical (ABC or BC rated), CO₂ (carbon dioxide), foam, and Class K wet chemical. ABC dry chemical extinguishers are the most common in workplaces because they work on Class A, B, and C fires. CO₂ extinguishers leave no residue but a fire may reignite if the burning material remains hot. Class K extinguishers are specifically designed for commercial cooking environments. Labels indicate which fire classes the extinguisher is rated for — always check the label before use.

pass-technique.title: The P.A.S.S. Technique
pass-technique.content: P.A.S.S. is the standard method for using a portable fire extinguisher: Pull the pin to unlock the handle. Aim the nozzle at the BASE of the fire, not at the flames or smoke. Squeeze the handle to discharge the agent. Sweep the nozzle from side to side while continuing to aim at the base of the fire. Always maintain your exit behind you and keep a safe distance from the fire. Never turn your back on a fire even after it appears to be out.

decision-making-fire.title: Decision-Making Before Using an Extinguisher
decision-making-fire.content: Not every fire should be fought with an extinguisher. Before attempting to suppress a fire, ensure the alarm has been activated and emergency procedures are in place, the fire is small and contained, you have the correct extinguisher for the fire class, a clear exit is behind you, and you are trained and authorized to fight fires. If any of these conditions cannot be met, evacuate immediately. The first priority is always protecting people, not property.

inspection-maintenance-fire.title: Inspection and Maintenance
inspection-maintenance-fire.content: Portable fire extinguishers must be visually inspected monthly and receive annual maintenance under 29 CFR 1910.157. Inspection points include checking that the extinguisher is in its designated location, is not obstructed or damaged, the pressure gauge reads in the operable range, the pin and tamper seal are intact, and the inspection tag is current. Employees should never test an extinguisher by briefly squeezing the handle — this can partially discharge the unit. Any deficiency, including an extinguisher that is blocked, damaged, or shows low pressure, must be reported immediately.

emergency-evacuation-fire.title: When to Evacuate Instead of Fight
emergency-evacuation-fire.content: Employees should always evacuate rather than attempt to fight a fire when: the fire is large or spreading rapidly, smoke is heavy and spreading, the correct extinguisher is not available, the exit path is blocked by fire or smoke, or they are not trained or authorized to fight fires. When in doubt, evacuate and follow the facility's emergency procedures. Report the fire location to emergency services and do not re-enter the building until cleared by authorities. Knowing when NOT to fight a fire is just as important as knowing how.

options.text: Open nearby doors to increase visibility

Move the trash can to another room
Open windows to clear smoke before acting

Evacuate immediately and report the condition
Stay and wait for someone else to bring an extinguisher
